subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: What Does Your Number Say About Your Neighbours?

textbook_items_in_class.description: List five different situations in which numbers are used. Share and discuss with classmates.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 3.1 p.56
textbook_items_in_class.description: For a group of 5 children, is the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 possible?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 3.1 p.56
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the sequence 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 possible? Why or why not?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.1 p.56
textbook_items_in_class.description: How would you rearrange the five children so that the maximum number of children say '2'?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 3.1 p.56
homework.description: There are 5 children all of different heights. Can they stand such that four say '1' and the last says '0'? Why or why not?

time_bands.activity: Math Talk, section 3.1 p.55 ("List five different situations in which numbers are used....") — students share examples aloud, establishing that numbers describe relationships, not just counts.

Whole-class guided reasoning: teacher poses the height-neighbour setup from section 3.1 — each child in a row announces how many immediate neighbours are taller. Students reason about what a child at an end can and cannot say, and why a child in the middle can say 0, 1, or 2. Figure it Out Q6, section 3.1 p.56 ("Is the sequence 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 possible? Why or why not?") is examined first as a shared example.

Pair work on Figure it Out Q5, section 3.1 p.56 ("For a group of 5 children, is the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 possible?") and Figure it Out Q7, section 3.1 p.56 ("How would you rearrange the five children so that the maximum number of children say '2'?"). Pairs articulate structural reasons — position constraints and relative ordering — before sharing with the class.
Class debrief: each pair states one constraint that makes a sequence impossible or possible, building a shared list of reasoning principles from the height-neighbour structure.

periods.teacher_notes: The central difficulty is distinguishing a constraint of position (end children have only one neighbour) from a constraint of relative order (two adjacent children of different heights cannot both say '2'). Watch for students who test sequences by trial without articulating why — press them with 'How do you know this arrangement is impossible?' to move from guessing to structural reasoning.
materials: Chalkboard or whiteboard for drawing the row of children
Blank paper for pair reasoning notes

periods.activity_title: Discovering Why the Largest Is Always a Supercell

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Colour or mark the supercells in the given table: 6828, 670, 9435, 3780, 3708, 7308, 8000, 5583, 52.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.2 p.58
textbook_items_in_class.description: Will the cell with the largest number always be a supercell? Can the cell with the smallest number be a supercell? Why or why not?
Can you fill a supercell table without repeating numbers such that there are no supercells? Why or why not?

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the supercell definition from section 3.2: a cell is a supercell if its number is strictly greater than every adjacent cell. Students examine Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.57 ("Colour or mark the supercells in the given table: 6828, 670, 9435....") and mark supercells individually, then compare with a neighbour.

Whole-class investigation of Figure it Out Q7, section 3.2 p.58 ("Will the cell with the largest number always be a supercell? Can the cell with the smallest number be a supercell?..."). Students reason in groups of three: they attempt to construct a counterexample to the first claim, discover it is impossible, and try to articulate the structural reason. Teacher guides the formalisation: the largest number has no neighbour that exceeds it, so it must be a supercell.

Groups tackle Try This Q6, section 3.2 p.58 ("Can you fill a supercell table without repeating numbers such that there are no supercells?..."). Through trial, students discover that a table with all distinct values must contain at least one supercell — the largest. Groups write a one-sentence justification.

Groups share their written justifications aloud. Teacher consolidates: the claim about the largest number and the impossibility of a supercell-free table with distinct values both follow from the same underlying argument.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'adjacent' with 'nearby' — clarify that adjacency in a row means only immediate left and right neighbours, while in a grid it includes top and bottom as well. A common error when attempting Try This Q6 is to repeat numbers, which the problem forbids; redirect students to the constraint before they proceed.
materials: Chalkboard
Squared or plain paper for constructing trial tables

periods.activity_title: Building Tables to Specification: Supercells by Design

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.2 p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table with only 4-digit numbers such that the supercells are exactly the pre-coloured cells (given seed values 5346, 1258, 9635).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 3.2 p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table to get as many supercells as possible using numbers between 100 and 1000 without repetitions.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 3.2 p.58
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill a table such that the cell having the second largest number is not a supercell.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 3.2 p.58
homework.description: Fill a table such that the second largest number is not a supercell but the second smallest number is a supercell. Is it possible?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.2 p.57 ("Fill the table with only 4-digit numbers such that the supercells are exactly the pre-coloured cells...."). Students work individually: they must place numbers so that exactly the pre-coloured positions are supercells and no other cell qualifies. The constraint requires careful comparison of each candidate cell with its neighbours.

Figure it Out Q3, section 3.2 p.57 ("Fill the table to get as many supercells as possible using numbers between 100 and 1000 without repetitions...."). Pairs compete to maximise supercell count, then discuss strategies: alternating large and small values, placing the largest at corners or edges. Figure it Out Q8, section 3.2 p.58 ("Fill a table such that the cell having the second largest number is not a supercell....") follows as a targeted constraint problem.

Class share-out: pairs present their maximum-supercell tables and their Q8 solutions. The class identifies which strategies reliably produce or deny supercell status for a given position, consolidating the application of the definition under varied constraints.

Teacher poses the homework question Figure it Out Q9, section 3.2 p.58 ("Fill a table such that the second largest number is not a supercell but the second smallest number is a supercell....") as a take-home challenge, reading it aloud and checking that every student understands the two simultaneous conditions.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that the largest number is always a supercell, students now apply that principle constructively — they must engineer a table rather than merely identify one. Watch for students who satisfy the pre-coloured cells in Q2 without checking that non-coloured cells are not accidentally also supercells; that second check is where most errors arise.
materials: Squared paper or printed table grids
Pencil and eraser for iterative table-filling

textbook_segments.title: Patterns of Numbers on the Number Line

periods.activity_title: Placing Large Numbers and Hunting Digit Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the numbers marked on four number lines at different scales and label the remaining positions. Sub-parts: (a) scale of 5; (b) scale of 1, around 9996–9997; (c) scale of 1, around 15077–15083; (d) scale of 1000, around 86705–87705.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.4 p.60
textbook_items_in_class.description: Digit sum 14: (a) write other numbers whose digits add up to 14; (b) smallest number with digit sum 14; (c) largest 5-digit number with digit sum 14; (d) how big a number can you form with digit sum 14?
Digit Detectives: among numbers 1–100, how many times does the digit '7' occur? Among 1–1000?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.59 ("Identify the numbers marked on four number lines at different scales...."). Students work independently on all four sub-parts, paying attention to how the scale changes the gap between consecutive ticks. After individual work, pairs check each other's labelling and identify the smallest and largest in each sub-part.

Transition to section 3.4: teacher establishes digit sum with the example from section 3.4 prose (68, 176, 545 all sum to 14). Students then work on Figure it Out Q1, section 3.4 p.60 ("Digit sum 14: write other numbers, find smallest, find largest 5-digit number...."), reasoning about how digit placement affects the size of a number while the sum stays fixed.

Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.61 ("Digit Detectives: how many times does '7' appear from 1–100?...."). Students work in pairs, first listing occurrences systematically by tens-place and units-place, then extending to 1–1000. Pairs share their counting strategies, highlighting the structural approach of separating place-value roles.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often read number-line tick marks without attending to the scale, placing a number between two ticks by eye rather than by computation — insist that they first determine what one tick-gap equals, then count. In the digit-sum work, the most common error is believing the smallest number with digit sum 14 must be a 2-digit number; ask students to check whether a 1-digit number is possible.
materials: Ruler (for number line drawing if needed)
Chalkboard for recording digit-sum examples

periods.activity_title: Reverse, Add, Repeat: Palindromes and Kaprekar's Magic

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write all possible 3-digit palindromes using the digits 1, 2, and 3.
Will reversing and adding numbers repeatedly, starting with a 2-digit number, always give a palindrome? Explore and find out.
Puzzle time: I am a 5-digit palindrome, odd, with 't' digit double 'u' digit and 'h' digit double 't' digit. Who am I?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.61 ("Write all possible 3-digit palindromes using the digits 1, 2, and 3...."). Students list palindromes individually, then the class collects and counts — this surfaces the structure: a 3-digit palindrome is determined entirely by its first and middle digits.

Math Talk, section 3.5 p.62 ("Will reversing and adding numbers repeatedly, starting with a 2-digit number, always give a palindrome?..."). Pairs each choose a 2-digit starting number, carry out the reverse-and-add process step by step, and record how many steps it takes. Results are pooled on the board; the class reasons about why the process terminates for 2-digit starts, and notes the exception flag for 196.

Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.62 ("Puzzle time: I am a 5-digit palindrome, odd, with 't' digit double 'u' digit and 'h' digit double 't' digit...."). Students work individually, setting up the digit constraints systematically before testing candidates — the palindrome structure (first digit = last, second = fourth) combined with the ratio constraints narrows the field quickly.

Class shares the puzzle answer and articulates the reasoning chain: palindrome symmetry + digit-ratio constraints + oddness together determine the number uniquely. Teacher notes the parallel structure in the Kaprekar section to be explored next.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently think 'palindrome' means only reading the same forwards and backwards without connecting this to place-value symmetry; use the 3-digit listing task to make the symmetry explicit before the reverse-and-add activity. In the puzzle, watch for students who satisfy the ratio conditions but forget the palindrome constraint — the two conditions must hold simultaneously.
materials: Chalkboard for pooling reverse-and-add results
Pencil and paper for systematic digit work

textbook_items_in_class.description: Take different 4-digit numbers and carry out the Kaprekar steps (form largest A and smallest B from digits, compute C = A − B, repeat). Find out what always happens.
Carry out the same Kaprekar steps with a few 3-digit numbers. What number starts repeating?
Find all possible times on a 12-hour clock of the type 4:44, 10:10 (two pairs), and 12:21 (palindrome time).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 3.7 p.65
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many rounds does the number 5683 take to reach the Kaprekar constant (6174)?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.63 ("Take different 4-digit numbers and carry out the Kaprekar steps...."). Each student chooses a different 4-digit starting number with at least two distinct digits, carries out the subtract-rearrange loop, and records how many steps to reach 6174. Results are written on the board — the class observes universal convergence. Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.63 ("Carry out the same Kaprekar steps with a few 3-digit numbers....") follows as a quick group extension to discover 495.

Figure it Out, section 3.7 p.64 ("Find all possible times on a 12-hour clock of the type 4:44, 10:10, and 12:21...."). Students work in pairs, systematically listing times under each pattern type and checking validity against clock constraints (hours 1–12, minutes 00–59).

Figure it Out Q4, section 3.7 p.65 ("How many rounds does the number 5683 take to reach the Kaprekar constant?..."). Students carry out the full computation, tallying rounds carefully. The class compares this round count with those gathered in the opening activity, observing that different starting numbers take different numbers of rounds but all arrive at 6174.

periods.teacher_notes: The Kaprekar procedure requires students to pad leading zeros when the subtraction result has fewer than four digits (e.g., 0999 must be treated as a 4-digit number in the next step) — this is the most common procedural error. When listing palindromic clock times, students often miss hours in the 10–12 range because the time format requires two digits for the hour; encourage systematic case-by-case checking.
materials: Chalkboard for posting convergence results
Pencil and paper for multi-step subtraction

periods.activity_title: Spider-Web Sums: Mental Strategies for Large Numbers

textbook_items_in_class.description: Spider-web mental math: the numbers in the middle column (400, 1500, 13000, 25000, 28000, 61600) can be added (each used as many times as needed) to reach target sums on the sides.
Adding and subtracting with the boxes (40000, 300, 7000, 1500, 12000, 800): use addition and subtraction to reach 45000, 5900, 17500, and 21400.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.8 p.67
textbook_items_in_class.description: Always, Sometimes, Never? (a) 5-digit + 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (b) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 4-digit number; (c) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 6-digit number; (d) 5-digit − 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (e) 5-digit − 2-digit gives a 3-digit number.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.8 p.66
homework.description: Write an example for each scenario: 5-digit + 5-digit > 90250; 5-digit + 3-digit = 6-digit; 4-digit + 4-digit = 6-digit; 5-digit + 5-digit = 6-digit; 5-digit + 5-digit = 18500; etc.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.8 p.65 ("Spider-web mental math: the numbers in the middle column can be added to reach target sums on the sides...."). Students work individually on the addition-only spider web, drawing arrows to show which central numbers they combine for each target. After individual attempts, pairs compare strategies and discuss why certain combinations work.

Figure it Out, section 3.8 p.66 ("Adding and subtracting with the boxes: use addition and subtraction to reach 45000, 5900, 17500, and 21400...."). With subtraction now permitted, students discover new routes to targets that addition alone could not reach. Groups of three compete to find the fewest-operation solution for each target.

Figure it Out Q2, section 3.8 p.67 ("Always, Sometimes, Never?..."). Students vote — always, sometimes, never — for each statement and then construct examples or counterexamples to justify their votes. The class debates cases where intuition is likely to mislead, particularly statements (b) and (e), which require boundary-case examples.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may struggle with the spider-web task by guessing rather than decomposing targets — encourage them to first identify which central value is closest to the target, then adjust. In the Always/Sometimes/Never activity, the common error is to mark 'always' for statements that are only sometimes true; push students to produce a single counterexample rather than accepting a plausible-sounding argument.
materials: Chalkboard for recording spider-web solutions
Pencil and paper for arithmetic working

textbook_segments.title: An Unsolved Mystery — the Collatz Conjecture!

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays: (a) 3×4 grid of 40s and 50s; (b) 3×5 grid of 40s and 50s; (c) 4×4 grid of 32s; (d) 4×4 grid of 32s and 64s; (e) diamond of 15s, 25s, 35s; (f) diamond of powers of 2.
Make Collatz sequences starting from your favourite whole numbers. Do you always reach 1? Do you believe Collatz's conjecture? Why or why not?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.9 p.67 ("Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays...."). Students work on sub-parts (a)–(c) individually: they may add one-by-one or use the count-and-multiply shortcut. After (a)–(c), the class compares methods — students who multiplied explain why their method works, developing the reasoning that equal values in an array need only be counted and scaled. Sub-parts (d)–(f) are attempted in pairs, with the diamond arrangements prompting new counting strategies.

Figure it Out, section 3.10 p.69 ("Make Collatz sequences starting from your favourite whole numbers. Do you always reach 1?..."). Each student picks a starting number, generates the sequence step by step, and records the length before reaching 1. Results are pooled on the board for a range of starting numbers. Students discuss: is it convincing evidence? What would it take to be certain? The unsolved status of the conjecture is foregrounded.

Whole-class reasoning discussion: students argue whether the evidence makes the conjecture believable and what kinds of starting numbers might be harder to check. Teacher surfaces the distinction between evidence and proof, connecting to the chapter's theme of mathematical reasoning versus algorithmic computation.

periods.teacher_notes: In the array-sum task, some students will insist on adding each number individually even when a shortcut is available — the pedagogical aim is for the class to articulate why multiplication is valid, not just to obtain the answer quickly. In the Collatz activity, students sometimes misapply the rule (halving odd numbers or tripling even ones); confirm the rule before they begin their sequences.
materials: Chalkboard for pooling Collatz sequence lengths
Pencil and paper for sequence generation

periods.activity_title: From Array Sums to Everyday Estimates

textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate the number of steps to walk: (a) to the classroom door; (b) across the school ground; (c) from classroom to school gate; (d) from school to home.
Estimate the number of times you blink or the number of breaths you take: (a) in a minute; (b) in an hour; (c) in a day.

Quick 30-second estimate questions: number of words in the maths textbook; school bus riders; Roshan's ₹100 estimate; Gandhinagar–Kohima distance; Sheetal's 13,000 school hours; walking time estimates; make your own estimation questions.

time_bands.activity: Brief bridge from section 3.9: teacher poses one fresh array-sum — a 5×3 arrangement of 25s — and asks students to find the total using the count-and-multiply reasoning developed in the previous work. Students respond quickly, confirming the shortcut. This grounds the section 3.9 application before the unit moves to estimation.

Figure it Out, section 3.11 p.69 ("Estimate the number of steps to walk to the classroom door, across the school ground....") and Figure it Out, section 3.11 p.70 ("Estimate blinks per minute, per hour, per day...."). Students first measure one reference count (blinks in 15 seconds, steps to the door), then scale up by multiplication — the same count-and-scale logic from array sums now applied to real quantities.

Figure it Out, section 3.11 p.70 ("Quick 30-second estimate questions: words in the maths textbook, bus riders, Gandhinagar–Kohima distance...."). Students answer each question in 30 seconds, then justify their reasoning aloud in pairs. The class debates the most contested estimates, and each student writes one original estimation question.

periods.teacher_notes: The deliberate bridge from array-sum counting to estimation scaling helps students see estimation not as guessing but as structured multiplication of a known small unit — name this connection explicitly. Watch for students who give single-digit or implausibly round estimates without a scaling argument; ask them to describe their reference unit before they scale.
materials: Chalkboard for recording class estimates
Pencil and paper for original estimation questions

periods.activity_title: Who Always Wins? Discovering Number-Game Strategies

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.12 p.72
textbook_items_in_class.description: Exchange two digits of one number to create exactly 4 supercells in the 3×3 grid.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 3.12 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Starting with 0, players alternate adding numbers between 1 and 3. The first person to reach 22 wins. What is the winning strategy now?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 3.12 p.72
textbook_items_in_class.description: Recall the powers of 2 from Chapter 1. Why is the Collatz conjecture correct for all starting numbers in this sequence?

time_bands.activity: Students play Game #1 from section 3.12 in pairs: alternately add 1, 2, or 3 to a running total; first to reach 21 wins. Three rounds per pair, with players swapping who goes first. After play, students record their observations about which player won and what moves felt decisive.

Class discussion: which starting positions guarantee a win? Students reason backwards from 21 — what total must you force your opponent to face? The target numbers 17, 13, 9, 5, 1 emerge inductively. Figure it Out Q10, section 3.12 p.73 ("Starting with 0, players alternate adding 1–3; first to reach 22 wins. What is the winning strategy?...") is then tackled: students apply the same backwards-reasoning method to the new target.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.12 p.72 ("Exchange two digits of one number to create exactly 4 supercells in the 3×3 grid...."). Students apply their supercell reasoning from section 3.2 in the consolidation grid, reasoning about which digit swap will propagate supercell status to the required positions. Figure it Out Q8, section 3.12 p.72 ("Why is the Collatz conjecture correct for all starting numbers that are powers of 2?...") is examined as a brief reasoning confirmation.

Whole-class close: students articulate one reasoning principle from the chapter — a constraint, a guaranteed property, or a winning condition — in a single sentence. Teacher collects these as a spoken survey, surfacing the range of structural reasoning the chapter has built.

periods.teacher_notes: The backwards-reasoning method for Game #1 is often the first time students encounter systematic backwards induction; some will identify the key numbers by trial-and-error play rather than logic — press those students to explain why those numbers are decisive, not just that they are. In Q1, students who have a firm grasp that the largest number is always a supercell will make the digit swap efficiently; those who do not will need to re-examine the supercell definition before proceeding.
materials: Chalkboard for recording target-number chains
Pencil and paper for grid digit-swap work

assessment_items.note: No goals routed to this section in the chapter.

items.prompt: Six children of all different heights stand in a line. The child at the left end says '1'. Explain why it is impossible for the child at the right end to say '2'. What is the maximum number the right-end child can say, and why?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The right-end child has only one immediate neighbour (the child just to their left). To say '2', both immediate neighbours must be taller — but an end child has only one neighbour, not two. Therefore the right-end child can say at most '1'.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the positional constraint that end children have exactly one neighbour, so their maximum announcement is 1.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the height-announcement rule and draw a small diagram of three children to count neighbours before answering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the left-end child says '1', what does that tell you about the relative heights of the first two children — and can you now say anything about what the second child must say?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 3.1 p.56
exercise.description: Is the sequence 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 possible? Why or why not?

items.prompt: A row of cells contains five different whole numbers. Priya claims: 'The cell with the smallest number can never be a supercell.' Is she correct? Justify your answer using the definition of a supercell.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is correct. A supercell must be strictly greater than every adjacent cell. The smallest number in the row has at least one neighbour, and every other number in the row is strictly greater than it. Therefore at least one of its neighbours is larger, so the smallest number cannot be greater than all its neighbours and cannot be a supercell.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the supercell definition: the smallest value cannot exceed any neighbour, so it fails the supercell condition.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to try a specific example — say, the row 3, 7, 12, 5, 9 — and check whether 3 qualifies as a supercell before generalising.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what if the row contained only one cell — would that single cell be a supercell? What does this reveal about the role of neighbours in the definition?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.2 p.58
exercise.description: Will the cell with the largest number always be a supercell? Can the cell with the smallest number be a supercell? Why or why not?

items.prompt: Arjun starts with the 2-digit number 47 and repeatedly applies the reverse-and-add procedure. After the first step he gets 47 + 74 = 121. He then claims: 'Every 2-digit starting number reaches a palindrome in exactly one step.' Which of the following is the best evaluation of his claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim cannot be evaluated because palindromes only exist for odd-digit numbers.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is correct because reversing and adding any 2-digit number always produces a 3-digit palindrome in one step.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is incorrect because no 2-digit number ever produces a palindrome through this procedure.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is incorrect because some 2-digit numbers require more than one reverse-and-add step before producing a palindrome.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — The claim is incorrect because some 2-digit numbers require more than one step. For example, 59 + 95 = 154, which is not a palindrome; a second step gives 154 + 451 = 605, still not a palindrome; a third gives 605 + 506 = 1111, which is. So 59 needs at least three steps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test a counterexample (e.g., 59) through the reverse-and-add procedure to show more than one step is sometimes needed.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student overgeneralised from a single example (like 47) and assumed one step is always sufficient without checking other cases.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student holds the misconception that the reverse-and-add procedure never produces palindromes, perhaps confusing it with the unsolved 196 exception.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has a misconception about what a palindrome is, believing digit count parity restricts palindrome formation.

inclusivity.support: Let the student try the procedure on 59 step by step, writing out each sum, before deciding on the answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a 2-digit number that reaches a palindrome in exactly two steps, and explain why a second step was needed.

exercise.description: Will reversing and adding numbers repeatedly, starting with a 2-digit number, always give a palindrome? Explore and find out.

items.prompt: A rectangular grid contains 4 rows and 6 columns, and every cell holds the number 35. Devika says she can find the total by counting the cells and multiplying by 35, without adding each cell separately. Explain why Devika's method gives the correct total, and state what the total is.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Devika's method is correct because every cell holds the same value (35), so the total is the same as adding 35 to itself as many times as there are cells. The number of cells is 4 × 6 = 24, and the total is 24 × 35 = 840.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the cells (4 × 6 = 24) and multiply by the repeated value (35) to get 840.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first find the total for a simpler 2 × 3 grid of 35s by adding, then compare with 6 × 35 to see they match.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the grid had two alternating values — 35 in odd-numbered cells and 70 in even-numbered cells — how would you adapt Devika's method to find the total efficiently?

exercise.description: Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays: (a) 3×4 grid of 40s and 50s; (b) 3×5 grid of 40s and 50s; (c) 4×4 grid of 32s; (d) 4×4 grid of 32s and 64s; (e) diamond of 15s, 25s, 35s; (f) diamond of powers of 2.

items.section_title: An Unsolved Mystery — the Collatz Conjecture!
items.prompt: The Collatz rule says: if a number is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1; repeat until you reach 1. Starting from 12, write the complete Collatz sequence. Then explain in your own words why mathematicians call this a 'conjecture' rather than a 'theorem', even though it has been checked for a very large number of starting values.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Starting from 12: 12 → 6 → 3 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. The sequence reaches 1 in 9 steps. The Collatz statement is a conjecture and not a theorem because no one has been able to prove it holds for every whole number — checking many cases provides evidence but not certainty. A single starting number that never reaches 1 would disprove it, and no proof ruling that out has been found.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the Collatz rule step by step (even → halve; odd → 3n+1) and then distinguish empirical evidence from mathematical proof.

inclusivity.support: Let the student work through the sequence one step at a time, writing whether each number is even or odd before applying the rule.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if you changed the rule to 'multiply by 5 and add 1' for odd numbers instead, do you think every starting number would still reach 1? Try a few cases and explain your thinking.

exercise.description: Make Collatz sequences starting from your favourite whole numbers. Do you always reach 1? Do you believe Collatz's conjecture? Why or why not?

items.prompt: Two players take turns adding 1, 2, or 3 to a running total that starts at 0. The first player to reach exactly 20 wins. Identify the winning strategy for the first player. List the key target totals the first player must reach, explain why reaching each target guarantees the win, and state what the first player's opening move should be.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The key target totals are 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20. If the first player always lands on a multiple of 4, the second player must add 1, 2, or 3, leaving a total of 4k+1, 4k+2, or 4k+3 — and the first player can always add enough to return to the next multiple of 4. Since 20 is a multiple of 4, the first player can guarantee reaching it. The opening move must be to say 0 — but 0 is already the start — so the first player must reach 4 on their first turn, meaning the opening move is to add 4; however, since only 1, 2, or 3 are allowed, the first player cannot reach 4 in one move. The correct analysis: 20 = 5 × 4, so working back, the targets are 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. The first player must reach 4 first. Since 0 is the start and 4 is 4 away, and 4 cannot be reached in one legal move, the first player cannot force a win — the second player holds the advantage. Target chain for second player: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. Second player's strategy: whatever first player adds (call it x), second player adds (4 − x) to reach the next multiple of 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from the target (20) in steps of 4 to identify key positions; the player who reaches each multiple of 4 controls the game.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first figure out: if the total is already 17, 18, or 19, which player wins on their next move — then extend this backwards thinking to 16.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the target were changed to 22 instead of 20, does the winning advantage shift? Work out the key targets for 22 and explain who now holds the winning strategy.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 3.12 p.73
exercise.description: Starting with 0, players alternate adding numbers between 1 and 3. The first person to reach 22 wins. What is the winning strategy now?

items.prompt: The single row below contains seven numbers. Identify all the supercells — cells whose value is strictly greater than every immediate neighbour — and write their values.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A cell is a supercell if it is strictly greater than both its immediate neighbours (or, for end cells, its single neighbour). Check each cell: 340 < 870 (not a supercell); 870 > 340 and 870 > 520 (supercell); 520 < 870 (not a supercell); 950 > 520 and 950 > 430 (supercell); 430 < 950 (not a supercell); 810 > 430 and 810 > 275 (supercell); 275 < 810 (not a supercell). The supercells are 870, 950, and 810.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each cell with its immediate left and right neighbours and mark those strictly greater than both.

inclusivity.support: Underline the neighbours of one cell at a time and write out the two comparisons explicitly before deciding.
inclusivity.challenge: Now add 60 to the value 430 and re-identify all supercells — does the change affect which cells qualify?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.2 p.57
exercise.description: Fill the table with only 4-digit numbers such that the supercells are exactly the pre-coloured cells (given seed values 5346, 1258, 9635).

items.section_title: Patterns of Numbers on the Number Line
items.prompt: A number line runs from 5000 to 6000. The line is divided into 10 equal parts. The tick marks are at 5000, 5100, 5200, …, 6000. Three numbers — 5350, 5780, and 5060 — are to be placed on this line. Between which two consecutive tick marks does each number lie? List your answers for all three numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each interval has width 100. 5350 lies between 5300 and 5400. 5780 lies between 5700 and 5800. 5060 lies between 5000 and 5100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Determine the tick-gap (100), then identify the two consecutive multiples of 100 that bound each number.

inclusivity.support: Write out the tick marks 5000, 5100, 5200, … on paper and locate each number by scanning the list.
inclusivity.challenge: If the same line were divided into 20 equal parts instead of 10, what would each tick-gap be, and between which two new ticks would 5350 fall?

exercise.description: Identify the numbers marked on four number lines at different scales and label the remaining positions. Sub-parts: (a) scale of 5; (b) scale of 1, around 9996–9997; (c) scale of 1, around 15077–15083; (d) scale of 1000, around 86705–87705.

items.prompt: Apply the Kaprekar process to the number 3087. Show each step: form the largest and smallest 4-digit arrangements of the digits, subtract to get a new number, and repeat until you reach a number you have seen before. How many steps does it take?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Digits of 3087: 8, 7, 3, 0. Step 1: largest = 8730, smallest = 0378 = 0378; 8730 − 0378 = 8352. Step 2: digits 8, 5, 3, 2; largest = 8532, smallest = 2358; 8532 − 2358 = 6174. Step 3: digits 7, 6, 4, 1; largest = 7641, smallest = 1467; 7641 − 1467 = 6174. Reached 6174 again at step 3, so the process converges to 6174 in 2 steps (reaching it first at step 2).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arrange the digits in descending and ascending order, subtract, and repeat; 3087 reaches 6174 in 2 steps.

inclusivity.support: Write the four digits on separate slips and physically arrange them largest-first and smallest-first before subtracting.
inclusivity.challenge: Try the same process starting from 5-digit number 54321 — does it converge to a fixed constant? What do you find after a few steps?

exercise.description: Take different 4-digit numbers and carry out the Kaprekar steps (form largest A and smallest B from digits, compute C = A − B, repeat). Find out what always happens.

items.prompt: The time on a 12-hour clock is 3:33. Find the next two times after 3:33 where the same digit appears in all positions displayed (hours and minutes, like 4:44). Write both times and the number of minutes between 3:33 and the first such time you find.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Times of the form h:hh (same digit in hours and minutes): valid hours are 1–12, valid minutes are 00–59. The single-digit repeated times are 1:11, 2:22, 3:33, 4:44, 5:55. After 3:33, the next is 4:44 (minutes elapsed: 4×60+44 − 3×60−33 = 264+44 − 180−33 = 308 − 213 = 71 minutes). The one after that is 5:55.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List valid same-digit clock times (1:11 through 5:55) and compute elapsed minutes from 3:33 to 4:44.

inclusivity.support: Write out all times of the form h:hh for h from 1 to 9 and check which are valid clock times before identifying the ones after 3:33.
inclusivity.challenge: Are there any valid same-digit times in the 10–12 hour range? Explain why or why not, considering that hours in that range have two digits.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 3.7 p.65
exercise.description: How many rounds does the number 5683 take to reach the Kaprekar constant (6174)?

items.prompt: Meera subtracts a 5-digit number from another 5-digit number. Her result has 4 digits. Which statement best describes this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: This can happen when the two 5-digit numbers are close together, so their difference is less than 10,000.

options.label: B
options.text: This can only happen when the larger number is exactly 10,000 more than the smaller number.

options.label: C
options.text: This is impossible because a 5-digit number is always at least 10,000 larger than any 4-digit number.

options.label: D
options.text: This is impossible because subtracting two 5-digit numbers always gives a 5-digit result.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B. For example, 10,001 − 10,000 = 1, a 1-digit result; or 15,000 − 11,200 = 3,800, a 4-digit result. When two 5-digit numbers are close, their difference can have fewer than five digits.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Construct a concrete example (e.g., 15000 − 11200 = 3800) to show the difference can be a 4-digit number.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student holds the misconception that the digit count of the result matches the digit count of the operands, ignoring that subtraction can drastically reduce the value.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses the boundary case (difference = 10,000, which is itself 5 digits) with the general condition, and over-specifies by requiring an exact difference.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates the minimum value of a 5-digit number (10,000) with the minimum possible difference between two 5-digit numbers, incorrectly concluding differences cannot be small.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to compute 12,000 − 11,500 and check how many digits the answer has before choosing.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a pair of 5-digit numbers whose difference is a 2-digit number, and a pair whose difference is a 1-digit number. What pattern do you notice about the pairs?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.8 p.67
exercise.description: Always, Sometimes, Never? (a) 5-digit + 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (b) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 4-digit number; (c) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 6-digit number; (d) 5-digit − 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (e) 5-digit − 2-digit gives a 3-digit number.

items.prompt: An array is arranged in a diamond shape with these values: the top position holds 120, the two middle positions each hold 60, and the three bottom positions each hold 30. Find the total sum of all values in the array, showing your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Count each value: one 120, two 60s, three 30s. Total = 1×120 + 2×60 + 3×30 = 120 + 120 + 90 = 330.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count occurrences of each distinct value, multiply each by its count, then add the products.

inclusivity.support: Write out each number in the array separately (120, 60, 60, 30, 30, 30) and add them one by one to verify the count-and-multiply result.
inclusivity.challenge: If you wanted a diamond array of the same shape with a total of 660, and the values must stay in the ratio 4:2:1 (top:middle:bottom), what values would each layer hold?

exercise.description: Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays: (a) 3×4 grid of 40s and 50s; (b) 3×5 grid of 40s and 50s; (c) 4×4 grid of 32s; (d) 4×4 grid of 32s and 64s; (e) diamond of 15s, 25s, 35s; (f) diamond of powers of 2.

items.prompt: A student counts that she takes about 80 steps per minute when walking at a normal pace. Estimate how many steps she takes on a school day if she walks for a total of about 15 minutes. Show the reasoning behind your estimate.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Steps per minute ≈ 80. Total walking time ≈ 15 minutes. Estimated steps = 80 × 15 = 1,200 steps. The reasoning: count a reference unit (steps per minute) and multiply by the number of units (minutes walked).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the known rate (80 steps per minute) by the estimated duration (15 minutes) to get approximately 1,200 steps.

inclusivity.support: First estimate steps for just 1 minute (80), then for 5 minutes, then for 15 minutes, building up in stages.
inclusivity.challenge: If the student walks the same 15 minutes every school day for a 5-day week, estimate the weekly step count and then the annual step count for 40 school weeks. Is your annual estimate more or less than 100,000 steps?

exercise.description: Quick 30-second estimate questions: number of words in the maths textbook; school bus riders; Roshan's ₹100 estimate; Gandhinagar–Kohima distance; Sheetal's 13,000 school hours; walking time estimates; make your own estimation questions.
